A Fine-Grained Analysis of the LoRA Fine-Tuning Landscape with Implications for Data Selection

Bowen Zhang Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong    Changrui Fang Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong    Xinsong Ma Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong    Jiaye Teng Affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics    Ziye Ma ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong
Abstract

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. Our central insight is that the appropriate adapter rank should depend on the quality of the data-induced optimization geometry, rather than on the model alone. To formalize this connection, we introduce LoRA-RIP, a data-dependent restricted-isometry metric that characterizes the conditioning of the cross-entropy (CE) objective along LoRA-relevant low-rank directions. We prove that sufficient rank over-parameterization, with the required rank explicitly determined by the LoRA-RIP constant, eliminates spurious local minima, thereby extending existing RIP-based guarantees beyond the classical 1/31/3 regime. This characterization further enables principled data selection under a fixed rank budget. Experiments across language and vision tasks support these theoretical predictions, showing that rank and data quality are two coupled resources that should be jointly considered for more efficient and reliable LoRA fine-tuning.

1 Introduction

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a standard parameter-efficient method for fine-tuning large models (Hu et al., 2022). Given a pretrained weight matrix W0∈ℝn1×n2W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, LoRA freezes W0W_{0} and learns an additive low-rank update W=W0+γ​MW=W_{0}+\gamma M, where M=U​V⊤M=UV^{\top}, U∈ℝn1×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times r}, V∈ℝn2×rV\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}\times r}, and γ\gamma is a scaling factor. With r≪min⁡(n1,n2)r\ll\min(n_{1},n_{2}), this factorization reduces the trainable parameter count for the adapted matrix from n1​n2n_{1}n_{2} to r⁡(n1+n2)r(n_{1}+n_{2}), lowering optimizer-state and memory requirements while often maintaining strong downstream performance. Realizing these efficiency gains, however, requires an appropriate choice of the adapter rank. Although larger ranks offer greater expressivity (Zeng and Lee, 2024), their practical value cannot be judged from representational capacity alone. In linearized fine-tuning experiments, Jang et al. (2024) observe that lower ranks converge more slowly even when they ultimately reach the same loss. Conversely, increasing rank need not improve downstream performance. For example, Albert et al. (2024) report that, when fine-tuning Phi3 on 15,000 examples, increasing the LoRA rank from 1616 to 3232 reduces the reported mean accuracy across eight commonsense reasoning tasks from 81.8%81.8\% to 80.3%80.3\%. These observations illustrate the cost of an unsuitable rank choice: an overly restrictive rank can slow optimization, whereas an unnecessarily large rank can consume additional resources without corresponding performance gains. Adaptive methods such as AdaLoRA improve the allocation of rank across weight matrices, but still require a prespecified target budget (Zhang et al., 2023). This leaves a complementary question: how should adapter rank be chosen to support effective fine-tuning without unnecessary parameter overhead?

This question naturally leads us to nonconvex low-rank optimization: LoRA learns a factorized update, with the adapter rank rr controlling its degree of parameterization (Burer and Monteiro, 2003). A long line of work has characterized the landscapes of factorized problems and established conditions excluding spurious local minima (Bhojanapalli et al., 2016; Ge et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021). In classical matrix sensing, the restricted isometry property (RIP) is a key metric that characterizes the optimization landscape, and it measures how uniformly the sensing data capture low-rank structure, making its constant a natural indicator of the underlying data geometry (Recht et al., 2010). More recent advances show that rank over-parameterization can improve the landscape by eliminating spurious local minima under weaker RIP conditions (Zhang, 2025a; Zhang, 2025b), directly connecting search rank with data-induced geometry. Classical sensing, however, assumes a fixed ℓ2\ell_{2} objective in matrix space, whereas LoRA settings have cross-entropy loss coupling with the base model structure. Its geometry therefore varies with the model’s responses to the data and the adapter update, making the extension of classical rank–RIP analysis nontrivial. Specifically for the LoRA fine-tuning landscape, Jang et al. (2024) establish no-spurious-minima guarantees in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime, while Liu et al. (2025) further relate adapter rank to local optimization geometry under ℓ2\ell_{2} loss. These results demonstrate the relevance of landscape theory, but their reliance on local linearization or squared-loss settings limits the guidance they provide for nonlinear cross-entropy fine-tuning. More recently, Kim et al. (2025) move beyond linearization by adapting established low-rank optimization arguments (Zhu et al., 2018; Ha et al., 2020), showing how RIP-type conditions still govern the landscapes in nonlinear LoRA settings and providing numerical evidence for their applicability. Their global-optimality guarantee in the analyzed region corresponds to a RIP constant below 1/31/3, while larger values allow a “fails-loudly” alternative. However, their analysis leaves two important aspects insufficiently characterized: the CE-specific structure of the RIP constant in LoRA, and how the adapter rank rr shapes the optimization landscape beyond the small-RIP regime. Since RIP is strongly determined by the geometry of the fine-tuning data, these two questions are closely connected: understanding LoRA optimization requires relating data-induced RIP to the role of rank in shaping the landscape. Clarifying this relationship is therefore a key step toward a more principled theory of rank choice in LoRA fine-tuning.

In this work, we build on theoretical tools from classical low-rank optimization and matrix sensing  (Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang, 2025b; Yalçın et al., 2023) and extend them to develop a fine-grained landscape characterization of LoRA under cross-entropy loss. We introduce a new data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant, denoted by δkLoRA\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}. Under the stated assumptions, we establish an explicit relation between r/r⋆r/r_{\star} and δkLoRA\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} that guarantees a landscape free of spurious local minima, where r⋆r_{\star} refers to the rank of the global solution. This implies that any algorithm that can converge to a second-order stationary point (SOSP)11 1 For definition of SOSP please see Appendix B.1 in polynomial time can reach the global solution reliably. More importantly, our results hold in the regime where δkLoRA\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} exceeds 1/31/3, and show that larger ranks permit larger LoRA-RIP values in the guarantee. Under common curvature bounds covering the ranks considered, this characterization yields a sufficient constant-factor rank requirement relative to r⋆r_{\star}, with the factor determined by the LoRA-RIP bound. Once this requirement is met, further rank is unnecessary for the same guarantee within that range. Therefore it means that in most LoRA settings, rr does not need to be excessively large to ensure good performance, preserving its parameter efficiency. Viewed from the data side, the same relationship suggests a complementary route to effective fine-tuning: improving the optimization geometry through data selection under a fixed rank budget. We therefore analyze the CE-specific structure of LoRA-RIP, revealing how certain properties of fine-tuning data affect its value and deriving corresponding data-selection principles. Together, these results connect rank requirements with data composition, providing theoretical guidance for choosing adapter rank and selecting data for more parameter-and data-efficient LoRA fine-tuning.

Main Contributions:
  • •

    We develop a theoretical framework linking adapter rank rr and a newly introduced notion LoRA-RIP δkLoRA\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} to global optimality in the balanced LoRA landscape. We show that as long as r/r⋆>(2​δkLoRA/(1−δkLoRA))2r/r_{\star}>\left(2\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}/(1-\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}})\right)^{2} , no spurious local minima exist in the landscape of Eq. (2), where r⋆r_{\star} denotes the rank of the global solution M∗M^{*} in Assumption3.1. This result establishes a sufficient rank threshold for a benign landscape. Our experiments further illustrate rank-dependent optimization trends consistent with this characterization.

  • •

    We identify theoretically motivated data-selection principles such as latent-space coverage and pre-tuning softmax saturation. Our analysis links data composition to LoRA-RIP and shows how more favorable data geometry reduces the amount of rank-over-parameterization needed for a benign landscape. This yields a landscape-guided view of data selection in which data quality and adapter rank act as complementary resources.

2 Related Work

LoRA methods and theory.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) has become a central parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, and numerous variants have been built on its structure, including quantized adapters (Dettmers et al., 2023), adaptive rank allocation (Zhang et al., 2023), and modified factor updates (Hayou et al., 2024). Other work studies geometric updates and stabilization mechanisms (Zhang and Pilanci, 2024; Yen et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2024). Recent theory has studied LoRA from complementary angles. Expressivity results characterize what a given adapter rank can represent (Zeng and Lee, 2024). From the view of optimization, NTK-regime analysis gives benign landscape guarantees for a linearized fine-tuning model (Jang et al., 2024). Other works analyze nonlinear LoRA landscapes or gradient-flow dynamics under structural assumptions  (Liu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025).

Low-rank optimization.

Low-rank matrix optimization provides a geometric foundation for understanding factorized objectives. A rank-constrained variable is often written as X=U​V⊤X=UV^{\top} by Burer-Monteiro factorization (Burer and Monteiro, 2003), which replaces the rank constraint by a nonconvex optimization problem over the factors. For matrix recovery and related objectives, restricted curvature or RIP-type conditions can imply benign landscape properties, such as the absence of spurious local minima or strict-saddle geometry  (Ge et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2018). Similar geometric analyses have also been developed for more general low-rank objectives (Zhang et al., 2021). A more recent direction studies rank over-parameterization: when the search rank exceeds the target rank r⋆r_{\star}, the required amount of over-parameterization can be expressed through RIP quantities (Zhang, 2025a; Zhang, 2025b).

Data selection and training geometry.

As innovations in model architecture hit a plateau, the strategic selection of training data becomes increasingly crucial. Existing work includes Shapley-based data valuation (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019; Wang et al., 2024), gradient-based data attribution and selection (Pruthi et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026) and similarity-based data filtering (Sachdeva et al., 2026; Das et al., 2026). Meanwhile, recent theoretical work explores the statistical properties (Allouah et al., 2026; Rezaei et al., 2026). Complementary work studies training geometry through Hessian spectra and cross-entropy dynamics  (Ghorbani et al., 2019; Garrod et al., 2025). In this work, we connect data composition to LoRA rank requirements through the optimization geometry of the cross-entropy objective.

3 Preliminaries

One-layer LoRA Fine-tuning

We freeze all pretrained parameters and apply a trainable LoRA update to a single weight matrix W0∈ℝn1×n2W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}. A LoRA update takes the form W=W0+M,M=U​V⊤,U∈ℝn1×r,V∈ℝn2×r.W=W_{0}+M,\quad M=UV^{\top},\quad U\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times r},\quad V\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}\times r}. The LoRA scaling factor can often be absorbed into the factors, so we adopt the normalized format M=U​V⊤M=UV^{\top} throughout. Given a training set S={(xi,yi)}i=1NS=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, define the empirical loss as L^​(M):=1N​∑i=1Nℓ⁡(fW0+M​(xi),yi)\widehat{L}(M):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell\bigl(f_{W_{0}+M}(x_{i}),y_{i}\bigr). With weight decay (λ>0)(\lambda>0) on the LoRA factors, the standard regularized LoRA objective is

h~λ​(U,V):=L^​(U​V⊤)+λ2​(‖U‖F2+‖V‖F2).\widetilde{h}_{\lambda}(U,V):=\widehat{L}(UV^{\top})+\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr). (1)

The factorizations are not unique: if RR is invertible, then (U​R,V​R−⁣⊤)(UR,VR^{-\top}) represents the same product as U​V⊤UV^{\top}. Thus the same product can have an infinite number of factorized representations. For the landscape analysis, we introduce a balancing term ‖U⊤​U−V⊤​V‖F2\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2} . This balancing term improves the factor-space geometry without restricting the set of representable updates. Such balancing principles are well established in asymmetric low-rank optimization and have recently been explored in LoRA  (Zhu et al., 2018; Castin et al., 2026). This leads to our main formulation:

hμ,λ​(U,V):=L^​(U​V⊤)+μ4​‖U⊤​U−V⊤​V‖F2+λ2​(‖U‖F2+‖V‖F2),h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V):=\widehat{L}(UV^{\top})+\frac{\mu}{4}\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr), (2)

where μ>0\mu>0 is the balancing weight. In Section 4, we first establish results for Eq. (2) and then transfer them back to the standard objective Eq. (1).

The Traditional Restricted Isometry Property(RIP) Notion

In classic matrix sensing, one often considers the quadratic loss of ‖𝒜⁡(M)−y‖22/2,\|\mathcal{A}(M)-y\|_{2}^{2}/2, where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a linear operator consisting of a number (for example mm) of sensing matrices {Ai}i=1m\{A_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} that each take an inner product with MM to give a mm-dimensional vector. Here we assume the target y=𝒜⁡(M∗)y=\mathcal{A}(M^{*}), the observation of the ground truth low-rank matrix M∗M^{*}. In such classical settings, it is well understood that the landscape and recovery guarantees are mostly determined by one metric, the restricted isometry property (RIP) constant  (Recht et al., 2010; Ge et al., 2017). We say 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies RIP with constant δk\delta_{k} if

(1−δk)​‖H‖F2≤‖𝒜⁡(H)‖22≤(1+δk)​‖H‖F2(1-\delta_{k})\|H\|_{F}^{2}\leq\|\mathcal{A}(H)\|_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k})\|H\|_{F}^{2}

for every low-rank matrix HH with rank⁡(H)≤k\operatorname{rank}(H)\leq k. The RIP constant can be understood as the conditioning of the Hessian restricted to the low-rank manifold of rank at most kk, with smaller values corresponding to more uniform restricted curvature. Under the simple ℓ2\ell_{2} loss, the Hessian will stay constant over the entire landscape, but for our LoRA objective Eq. (2), Hessians vary across points, complicating direct RIP-based arguments.

Low-rank global minimizer exists

One important distinction between our LoRA formulation and classical low-rank matrix recovery is that LoRA does not assume the existence of a “ground-truth” matrix M∗M^{*}. Nevertheless, the optimization objective is analogous: in both settings, we seek global minima because they correspond to the best achievable empirical fit and, ultimately, the solutions expected to yield the strongest performance. In low-rank recovery, this target coincides with the ground-truth matrix M∗M^{*} by construction, whereas in LoRA fine-tuning it corresponds to the globally optimal low-rank adaptation under the training objective. Motivated by evidence that fine-tuning can exploit low-dimensional parameterizations  (Aghajanyan et al., 2021), we make the following assumption that the global solution to the matrix lasso objective Fλ​(M)F_{\lambda}(M) has rank r⋆r_{\star}, which is lower than the LoRA search rank rr:

Assumption 3.1 (Existence of low-rank global minimizer).
M⋆λ∈argminM∈ℝn1×n2Fλ​(M),rank⁡(M⋆λ)=r⋆,r≥r⋆.M_{\star}^{\lambda}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}}F_{\lambda}(M),\quad\operatorname{rank}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})=r_{\star},\quad r\geq r_{\star}. (3)

Here, Fλ​(M):=L^​(M)+λ​‖M‖∗F_{\lambda}(M):=\widehat{L}(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*} is the matrix lasso formulation of the main objective hμ,λ​(U,V)h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V), and in Appendix B.2 we prove that infU,Vhμ,λ​(U,V)=infrank⁡(M)≤rFλ​(M)\inf_{U,V}h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V)=\inf_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r}F_{\lambda}(M).

4 LoRA-RIP and Rank Thresholds for Benign Landscape

4.1 Definition of LoRA-RIP

Assumption 4.1 (Rank-kk restricted strong convexity / restricted strong smoothness (RSC/RSS)).

For a candidate LoRA update M=U​V⊤M=UV^{\top}, define the line segment as Mt=M⋆λ+t⁡(M−M⋆λ)M_{t}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t(M-M_{\star}^{\lambda}), t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. For a fixed rank order k≥r+r⋆k\geq r+r_{\star}, assume that L^\widehat{L} has restricted curvature bounds 0<αk≤βk<∞0<\alpha_{k}\leq\beta_{k}<\infty along this segment:

αk​‖H‖F2≤⟨∇2L^​(Mt)​[H],H⟩≤βk​‖H‖F2\alpha_{k}\|H\|_{F}^{2}\leq\langle\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M_{t})[H],H\rangle\leq\beta_{k}\|H\|_{F}^{2} (4)

for all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and all directions HH with rank⁡(H)≤k\operatorname{rank}(H)\leq k.

LoRA-RIP constant

Under Assumption 4.1, we define the rank-kk LoRA-RIP constant by

δkLoRA:=βk−αkβk+αk.\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}:=\frac{\beta_{k}-\alpha_{k}}{\beta_{k}+\alpha_{k}}.

For clarity, we state the main result with the balancing weight μ=αk/2\mu=\alpha_{k}/2. The corresponding guarantee for general 0<μ<αk0<\mu<\alpha_{k} is given in Appendix B.3.2.

Proposition 4.3 (Stationarity of standard LoRA implies balance).

Let (U,V)(U,V) be a first-order stationary point of the standard LoRA objective in  Eq. (1). Then U⊤​U=V⊤​V.U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V. Consequently, if (U,V)(U,V) is a second-order stationary point of  Eq. (1), then it is also a second-order stationary point of the balanced objective in  Eq. (2).

Combining Theorem 4.2 with Proposition 4.3 gives the following transfer.

Corollary 4.4 (Global optimality of SOSPs for standard LoRA).

Under Assumption 3.1 and the rank condition of Theorem 4.2, every SOSP of the standard LoRA objective Eq. (1) whose product satisfies Assumption 4.1 with the same constants is globally optimal and satisfies U​V⊤=M⋆λUV^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}.

The proofs of Proposition 4.3 and Corollary 4.4 are given in Appendix B.4. The rank condition reveals a continuous tradeoff between parameterization and restricted geometry, rather than only a single sufficient threshold. For a fixed LoRA-RIP level, it quantifies how much rank over-parameterization is sufficient to exclude spurious local minima. Conversely, for a fixed adapter rank, the condition can be written as δkLoRA<r/r⋆2+r/r⋆,\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}<\frac{\sqrt{r/r_{\star}}}{2+\sqrt{r/r_{\star}}}, showing that additional rank enlarges the range of restricted geometries covered by the guarantee. This dual view also makes the role of data geometry explicit: improving restricted conditioning reduces the amount of parameterization needed for the same global-optimality guarantee. Thus rank and data-induced geometry act as complementary resources in shaping the LoRA optimization landscape.

5 Towards Improved Data Selection via Landscape Analysis

5.1 Decomposition of the LoRA-RIP metric

We next explain how the LoRA-RIP condition depends on the choice of training data. Let ν\nu denote the empirical distribution over the supervised prediction instances used for fine-tuning. Changing the dataset, reweighting groups, or duplicating examples can be represented as changing ν\nu, and therefore changes the empirical cross-entropy objective

L^ν​(M):=𝔼x∼ν​[−⟨qx,log⁡softmax⁡(zx​(M))⟩].\widehat{L}_{\nu}(M):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}\left[-\left\langle q_{x},\log\operatorname{softmax}(z_{x}(M))\right\rangle\right]. (7)

Here zx​(M)∈ℝKz_{x}(M)\in\mathbb{R}^{K} is the pre-softmax logit vector produced by the model with LoRA update matrix MM, qxq_{x} is the target distribution, and px​(M)=softmax⁡(zx​(M))p_{x}(M)=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{x}(M)). This formulation is important because the curvature constants in the landscape theorem are exactly curvature constants of L^ν\widehat{L}_{\nu} along low-rank LoRA directions. Thus the LoRA-RIP constant is not only a property of the architecture; it also depends on which examples are averaged in L^ν\widehat{L}_{\nu}. We write Mν,⋆λM_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda} for the corresponding regularized target in Assumption 3.1, and rν,⋆:=rank⁡(Mν,⋆λ)r_{\nu,\star}:=\operatorname{rank}(M_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda}). For a LoRA direction HH, define the first-order logit response Ax,M​[H]:=D​zx​(M)​[H].A_{x,M}[H]:=Dz_{x}(M)[H]. Since cross-entropy is invariant to adding the same constant to every logit, only the centered response P⟂​Ax,M​[H]P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H], with P⟂=I−𝟏𝟏⊤/KP_{\perp}=I-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}/K, contributes meaningful curvature. We measure how well the data observe the direction HH by Qν​(M,H):=𝔼x∼ν​‖P⟂​Ax,M​[H]‖22.Q_{\nu}(M,H):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}\|P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H]\|_{2}^{2}. Large Qν​(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H) means that the selected data are sensitive to this LoRA direction; small Qν​(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H) means that the direction is nearly invisible. Good data should therefore give a large coverage floor over all relevant low-rank directions, without placing excessive curvature on only a few dominant directions. For cross-entropy, the Hessian decomposes into a Gauss–Newton term and a residual term:

⟨∇2L^ν​(M)​[H],H⟩=Gν​(M,H)+Rν​(M,H).\left\langle\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}_{\nu}(M)[H],H\right\rangle=G_{\nu}(M,H)+R_{\nu}(M,H). (8)

To define these terms, let

ℬx,M​[H,H]:=D2​zx​(M)​[H,H],Ωx​(M):=Diag⁡(px​(M))−px​(M)​px​(M)⊤.\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H]:=D^{2}z_{x}(M)[H,H],\qquad\Omega_{x}(M):=\operatorname{Diag}(p_{x}(M))-p_{x}(M)p_{x}(M)^{\top}.

Here ℬx,M​[H,H]\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H] is the second-order logit response, and Ωx​(M)\Omega_{x}(M) is the softmax covariance. Then

Gν​(M,H)\displaystyle G_{\nu}(M,H) :=𝔼x∼ν​⟨Ax,M​[H],Ωx​(M)​Ax,M​[H]⟩,\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}\langle A_{x,M}[H],\Omega_{x}(M)A_{x,M}[H]\rangle,
Rν​(M,H)\displaystyle R_{\nu}(M,H) :=𝔼x∼ν​⟨px​(M)−qx,ℬx,M​[H,H]⟩.\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}\langle p_{x}(M)-q_{x},\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H]\rangle.

The term GνG_{\nu} captures curvature created by first-order logit changes, weighted by the local softmax covariance. The term RνR_{\nu} is the residual Hessian term caused by the nonlinearity of the logit map M↦zx​(M)M\mapsto z_{x}(M). In particular, if the logits were affine in MM, then ℬx,M​[H,H]=0\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H]=0, and hence Rν​(M,H)=0R_{\nu}(M,H)=0. Highly concentrated softmax predictions limit the softmax-side weighting of first-order responses, motivating the joint consideration of saturation and directional coverage (see Appendix C.2 and Appendix C.6).

For fixed ν\nu, rr, over the admissible family 𝒯k​(ν,r)\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r), defined precisely in Appendix C, we summarize the data-side curvature by five quantities. The constants cν,kc_{\nu,k} and Cν,kC_{\nu,k} are the minimum and maximum of the coverage Qν​(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H). Thus cν,kc_{\nu,k} is the weakest observed LoRA-relevant direction, while Cν,kC_{\nu,k} measures the strongest observed direction. The constants ων,k−\omega_{\nu,k}^{-} and ων,k+\omega_{\nu,k}^{+} measure the lower and upper softmax-weighting strength on these observed logit responses, and ρν,k\rho_{\nu,k} bounds the residual term RνR_{\nu}. The data-side restricted curvature condition is

cν,k>0,0<ων,k−≤ων,k+<∞,ρν,k<ων,k−​cν,k.c_{\nu,k}>0,\qquad 0<\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}\leq\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}<\infty,\qquad\rho_{\nu,k}<\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}.

This is a restricted observability condition, not a global strong-convexity assumption for cross-entropy. It only requires the selected data to see the low-rank LoRA directions used by the theorem, and it requires the residual Hessian term to stay below the Gauss–Newton curvature floor. Under this condition, the cross-entropy loss has valid restricted curvature constants

αν,kCE=ων,k−​cν,k−ρν,k,βν,kCE=ων,k+​Cν,k+ρν,k.\alpha_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{CE}}=\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}-\rho_{\nu,k},\qquad\beta_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{CE}}=\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\rho_{\nu,k}.

Substituting these constants into the LoRA-RIP normalization gives the conservative certificate

δν,kLoRA≤δ¯ν,kLoRA:=ων,k+​Cν,k−ων,k−​cν,k+2​ρν,kων,k+​Cν,k+ων,k−​cν,k.\delta_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}\leq\overline{\delta}_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}:=\frac{\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}-\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}+2\rho_{\nu,k}}{\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}}. (9)

Thus data selection can improve the LoRA-RIP certificate by increasing the weakest observed LoRA-relevant directions, avoiding excessive concentration on a few dominant directions, and reducing the residual nonlinear curvature. Duplicate or imbalanced data can hurt because they reinforce already-visible directions instead of improving the missing-direction floor, formalized in Appendix C.4.

5.2 Data Selection Criteria Based on LoRA-RIP

The certificate above turns data selection into the problem of improving the data-side LoRA-RIP certificate, which leads to several selection rules we discuss below:

Latent-space coverage.

Here latent-space coverage refers to whether hidden-state directions are both sensitive to data change and visible through the downstream Jacobian in the projected logit space. Coverage primarily affects cν,kc_{\nu,k} and Cν,kC_{\nu,k}. For a rank-one direction H=u​v⊤H=uv^{\top}, with u∈ℝn1u\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} and v∈ℝn2v\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}, Ax,M​[u​v⊤]=Jx,M​u​⟨v,ax​(M)⟩,A_{x,M}[uv^{\top}]=J_{x,M}u\langle v,a_{x}(M)\rangle, where ax​(M)∈ℝn2a_{x}(M)\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}} is the hidden state entering this matrix, and Jx,M∈ℝK×n1J_{x,M}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times n_{1}} is the Jacobian from the adapted-layer output to the logits. Therefore,

Qν​(M,u​v⊤)=𝔼ν​[⟨v,ax​(M)⟩2​‖P⟂​Jx,M​u‖22].Q_{\nu}(M,uv^{\top})=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\left[\langle v,a_{x}(M)\rangle^{2}\,\|P_{\perp}J_{x,M}u\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (10)

This formula shows that coverage has two sides: the selected examples must excite the input-side hidden direction vv, and the downstream Jacobian must make the output-side direction uu visible in the shift-orthogonal logit space. If a direction is weakly represented, then Qν​(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H) can be small and cν,kc_{\nu,k} decreases. If examples are repeatedly drawn from the same mode, Cν,kC_{\nu,k} can increase without improving cν,kc_{\nu,k}, which worsens the LoRA-RIP certificate.

This perspective can be formalized through group-balanced selection. Suppose νπ=∑g=1Gπg​νg\nu_{\pi}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}\nu_{g} is a mixture over groups formed by hidden-state, gradient, or logit-response similarity, where g∈{1,…,G}g\in\{1,\ldots,G\} indexes groups of examples, νg\nu_{g} is the empirical distribution within group gg, and πg≥0\pi_{g}\geq 0 is the sampling mass assigned to that group with ∑g=1Gπg=1\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}=1. Then, for fixed M,HM,H,

Qνπ​(M,H)=∑g=1Gπg​Qνg​(M,H).Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum\nolimits_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}Q_{\nu_{g}}(M,H).

Appendix C.4 formalizes how such group masses affect the coverage floor and ceiling. Although the infimum and supremum defining cν,kc_{\nu,k} and Cν,kC_{\nu,k} do not decompose linearly, this identity shows how group weights move curvature mass across directions. Increasing the weight of groups that cover weak directions can raise cν,kc_{\nu,k}; oversampling redundant groups can mainly raise Cν,kC_{\nu,k}. This motivates allocating data across complementary response groups while avoiding severe undercoverage. We use approximately balanced group quotas as a practical implementation of this principle in our experiments. The clustering criteria shall be proxies for LoRA-relevant low-rank directions, such as hidden states, gradients with respect to the adapted matrix, or projected logit-response sketches. In Section 6, we use the gradient sketches as the practical proxy. Appendix C.5 explains why such sketches are aligned with the Gauss–Newton coverage operator.

Softmax saturation.

Saturation primarily affects ων,k−\omega_{\nu,k}^{-} and ων,k+\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}. The relevant object is the softmax covariance Ωx​(M)\Omega_{x}(M), not the loss value alone. For any logit response s=Ax,M​[H]s=A_{x,M}[H], the Gauss–Newton contribution is ⟨s,Ωx​(M)​s⟩\langle s,\Omega_{x}(M)s\rangle, which is upper bounded by λmax​(Ωx​(M))​‖s‖22\lambda_{\max}(\Omega_{x}(M))\|s\|_{2}^{2}. Therefore, when Ωx​(M)\Omega_{x}(M) is small, the same covered direction produces only weak softmax-weighted curvature. If pmax=1−ϵp_{\max}=1-\epsilon, then

λmax​(Ωx​(M))≤tr⁡(Ωx​(M))=1−‖px​(M)‖22≤2​ϵ−ϵ2.\lambda_{\max}(\Omega_{x}(M))\leq\operatorname{tr}(\Omega_{x}(M))=1-\|p_{x}(M)\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\epsilon-\epsilon^{2}.

Appendix C.6 gives the variance identity behind Ωx​(M)\Omega_{x}(M) and the corresponding curvature-leverage bound. Thus highly confident examples contribute little softmax-weighted curvature even if their LoRA-relevant directions are covered; they can reduce ων,k−\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}. On the other hand, extremely ambiguous examples are not automatically optimal: their curvature may concentrate on already-covered directions, increasing ων,k+​Cν,k\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}, or they may correspond to noisy examples that increase the residual gap. These observations motivate confidence-aware selection alongside directional coverage, favoring examples that provide nontrivial softmax curvature without excessively concentrating it on a few directions.

6 Experiments

We run some numerical experiments to validate our qualitative view on data selection and landscape results. Relevant code can be found in the supplementary materials.

Experimental setup.

We consider one language task and one vision task. For NLP, we fine-tune MPNet-base  (Song et al., 2020) on MNLI (Williams et al., 2018), a natural-language inference task in GLUE (Wang et al., 2018). For vision, we fine-tune a ViT-B/16 model  (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) on CIFAR-100 (Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009). In each run, we apply LoRA to the query projection in layer/block 10. Each experiment controls all other training choices except for the single factor being tested. Full protocols and complete results for the main-text experiments are provided in Appendix D. We further offer curvature diagnostics, multi-seed evaluations, and robustness studies across datasets and adaptation settings in Appendix E.

Rank sweep.

The rank sweep isolates the role of the search rank while keeping the data distribution fixed. Because our theory concerns the cross-entropy objective rather than classification accuracy alone, we report validation CE as the primary metric. Figure 1 shows an extended sweep over r∈{1,4,16,32,64,128,256,512}r\in\{1,4,16,32,64,128,256,512\}. Increasing rank leads to clear reductions in validation CE on MNLI, while the gains on CIFAR-100 are considerably smaller, although higher ranks still provide modest improvements overall. These trends are qualitatively consistent with the optimization role of rank highlighted by our rank–LoRA-RIP analysis. The landscape diagnostics in Appendix E.2 provide complementary evidence: higher-rank runs reach lower-loss states with more favorable local second-order geometry in the shared diagnostic subspace. Together, these results connect the empirical effect of rank to the optimization perspective developed in our theory.

Gradient-coverage intervention.

The second experiment tests the data-selection prediction from Section 5.2 on MNLI. We keep the subset size and label counts fixed, and change only how examples are distributed across gradient groups. These groups are built from a random-projected margin-Jacobian feature at the adapted matrix, so they act as a practical proxy for which LoRA directions the data cover; see Appendix C.5. We compare balanced coverage with light and heavy long-tail coverage. Figure 2 shows that balanced coverage performs best overall. Long-tail sampling hurts validation accuracy, especially under heavy long-tail sampling and at smaller ranks. This matches the LoRA-RIP view: if too many examples come from the same gradient groups, the data repeatedly cover the same directions while leaving other useful directions weakly observed. In the notation of Section 5.2, this worsens the balance between the coverage floor cν,kc_{\nu,k} and ceiling Cν,kC_{\nu,k}.

The gap shrinks as rank increases. By r=64r=64, balanced and light long-tail sampling have similar validation accuracy, although balanced sampling still gives better test accuracy. The remaining gains at larger ranks underscore the complementary roles of adapter rank and data composition, consistent also with our landscape results. Additional multi-seed robustness and curvature diagnostics are provided in Appendices E.4, E.5, and E.6.

Saturation-band intervention.

The third experiment evaluates confidence-aware selection while keeping subset size, label counts, and gradient-group quotas fixed. Within each group, we select easy, middle, or near-boundary examples using the shared reference model; Appendix D.5 describes the construction. Figure 3 shows that both Middle and Boundary outperform Easy in the controlled MNLI comparison. The multi-seed results in Appendix E.7 also show higher mean validation accuracy for both less-saturated bands than for Easy at every tested rank, while their relative ordering varies with rank. These performance results are qualitatively consistent with the limited softmax-side curvature leverage of highly saturated examples in Section 5.2. The practical implication is to use confidence alongside directional coverage and avoid concentrating the data budget on highly saturated examples.

7 Conclusion

We studied how adapter rank and fine-tuning data jointly shape LoRA’s optimization landscape under cross-entropy loss. Under the stated assumptions, rank over-parameterization relative to the target rank rules out spurious local minima, with the required factor explicitly determined by our data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant δkLoRA\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}. The guarantee also covers LoRA-RIP values above 1/31/3, quantifying how additional rank can compensate for less favorable geometry to achieve a benign landscape. Our framework further motivates data selection under a fixed rank budget, yielding principles based on latent-space coverage and pre-tuning softmax saturation. Experiments support these insights into the interplay between rank and data composition. However, most of the bounds presented in this work are sufficient, and an important future direction is to shorten their gap with necessary ones.

Appendix B Detailed Proofs for Sections 3 and 4

B.1 Stationarity notions

Let g:ℝm×n→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R} be twice-continuously differentiable. We say that Y∈ℝm×nY\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is a first-order stationary point if ∇g​(Y)=0.\nabla g(Y)=0. We say that Y∈ℝm×nY\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is a second-order stationary point (SOSP) if ∇g​(Y)=0\nabla g(Y)=0 and ∇2g​(Y)​[H,H]≥0\nabla^{2}g(Y)[H,H]\geq 0 for any direction H∈ℝm×n.H\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. We say that YY is a local minimum if there exists an open ball BB containing YY such that g⁡(Y)≤g⁡(Y′)g(Y)\leq g(Y^{\prime}) for every Y′∈BY^{\prime}\in B. YY is a global minimum if g⁡(Y)≤g⁡(Y′)g(Y)\leq g(Y^{\prime}) for every Y′∈ℝm×nY^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. A spurious local minimum is a local minimum that is not global. A standard result shows that gradient descent with random initialization avoids strict saddles almost surely; when the iterates converge, this makes SOSPs the relevant local optimality objects  [Lee et al., 2016]. In particular, every local minimum is an SOSP.

B.2 Proof that l2l_{2} regularization induces a nuclear-norm target

Proof.

Fix a matrix M∈ℝn1×n2M\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} with rank⁡(M)≤r\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r. For every factorization U​V⊤=MUV^{\top}=M, the balancing term is nonnegative, and the standard variational characterization of the nuclear norm gives

‖M‖∗≤12​(‖U‖F2+‖V‖F2).\|M\|_{*}\leq\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr).

Therefore

μ4​‖U⊤​U−V⊤​V‖F2+λ2​(‖U‖F2+‖V‖F2)≥λ​‖M‖∗.\frac{\mu}{4}\,\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\geq\lambda\|M\|_{*}.

Taking the infimum over all pairs (U,V)(U,V) with U​V⊤=MUV^{\top}=M yields the lower bound

infU,V:U​V⊤=M[μ4∥U⊤U−V⊤V∥F2+λ2(∥U∥F2+∥V∥F2)]≥λ∥M∥∗.\inf_{U,V:\,UV^{\top}=M}\left[\frac{\mu}{4}\,\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\right]\geq\lambda\|M\|_{*}.

To prove the reverse inequality, let

M=P​Σ​Q⊤M=P\Sigma Q^{\top}

be a compact SVD, where Σ∈ℝs×s\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times s} and s=rank⁡(M)≤rs=\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r. Define the square-root lift

U:=[P​Σ1/2, 0n1×(r−s)],V:=[Q​Σ1/2, 0n2×(r−s)].U:=[P\Sigma^{1/2},\,0_{n_{1}\times(r-s)}],\qquad V:=[Q\Sigma^{1/2},\,0_{n_{2}\times(r-s)}].

Then U​V⊤=MUV^{\top}=M, and

U⊤​U=V⊤​V=diag⁡(Σ,0r−s),U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma,0_{r-s}),

so the balancing penalty vanishes. Moreover,

λ2​(‖U‖F2+‖V‖F2)=λ2​(tr⁡Σ+tr⁡Σ)=λ​tr⁡(Σ)=λ​‖M‖∗.\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma\bigr)=\lambda\,\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\lambda\|M\|_{*}.

Hence the infimum over factorizations with fixed product MM is λ​‖M‖∗\lambda\|M\|_{*}.

Now minimize first over all factor pairs with fixed product MM, and then over all matrices with rank⁡(M)≤r\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r. This gives

infU,Vhμ,λ​(U,V)=infrank⁡(M)≤r[L^​(M)+λ​‖M‖∗]=infrank⁡(M)≤rFλ​(M),\inf_{U,V}h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V)=\inf_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r}\bigl[\widehat{L}(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*}\bigr]=\inf_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r}F_{\lambda}(M),

which is the matrix-space equivalence used in the main text. ∎

B.3 Detailed Proof of Theorem 4.2

The proof is organized around one lifted error matrix. We compare the candidate factors with the balanced lift of the regularized matrix target, and then show that any nonzero lifted error creates a descent-or-negative-curvature certificate. This is why the proof is carried out in the stacked factor variable XX, rather than directly in the product U​V⊤UV^{\top}: the SOSP condition is a factor-space condition, while the curvature assumption is a matrix-space condition. The stacked notation lets us pass between the two.

We retain a general balancing weight 0<μ<αk0<\mu<\alpha_{k} throughout the certificate construction and specialize to μ=αk/2\mu=\alpha_{k}/2 when concluding the main theorem. The corresponding general-μ\mu guarantee is stated in Appendix B.3.2.

Throughout this subsection, fix a candidate pair (U,V)(U,V), write

M:=U​V⊤,Δ:=M−M⋆λ,X:=[UV],Z:=[U⋆V⋆],E:=X​X⊤−Z​Z⊤,M:=UV^{\top},\qquad\Delta:=M-M_{\star}^{\lambda},\qquad X:=\begin{bmatrix}U\\ V\end{bmatrix},\qquad Z:=\begin{bmatrix}U_{\star}\\ V_{\star}\end{bmatrix},\qquad E:=XX^{\top}-ZZ^{\top},

and let

J:=diag⁡(In1,−In2).J:=\operatorname{diag}(I_{n_{1}},-I_{n_{2}}).

Recall that U⋆​V⋆⊤=M⋆λU_{\star}V_{\star}^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda} and U⋆⊤​U⋆=V⋆⊤​V⋆U_{\star}^{\top}U_{\star}=V_{\star}^{\top}V_{\star}, so

Z⊤​J​Z=0.Z^{\top}JZ=0.

If E=0E=0, then the (1,2)(1,2)-block of X​X⊤=Z​Z⊤XX^{\top}=ZZ^{\top} already gives U​V⊤=M⋆λUV^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}. The proof therefore assumes E≠0E\neq 0 and derives a contradiction with second-order stationarity.

KKT slack for the regularized target.

The theorem targets the nuclear-norm-regularized matrix-space minimizer M⋆λM_{\star}^{\lambda}, so the correct stationarity condition is a KKT condition rather than ∇L^​(M⋆λ)=0\nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})=0. The slack form below is the device that keeps the regularized target in the proof: it creates a positive-semidefinite term that vanishes on the target lift ZZ, and hence can only help when we upper-bound the certificate.

Proposition B.1 (KKT slack form of the regularized target).

There exists a matrix

S⋆=P⋆​Q⋆⊤+W⋆∈∂‖M⋆λ‖∗S_{\star}=P_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}+W_{\star}\in\partial\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}

such that

∇L^​(M⋆λ)+λ​S⋆=0,\nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\lambda S_{\star}=0, (11)

where

P⋆⊤​W⋆=0,W⋆​Q⋆=0,‖W⋆‖op≤1.P_{\star}^{\top}W_{\star}=0,\qquad W_{\star}Q_{\star}=0,\qquad\|W_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1.

If

S~⋆:=[0S⋆S⋆⊤0],\widetilde{S}_{\star}:=\begin{bmatrix}0&S_{\star}\\ S_{\star}^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix},

then

I−S~⋆⪰0,(I−S~⋆)​Z=0.I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}\succeq 0,\qquad(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star})Z=0. (12)
Proof.

Since M⋆λM_{\star}^{\lambda} minimizes Fλ​(M)=L^​(M)+λ​‖M‖∗F_{\lambda}(M)=\widehat{L}(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*} and L^\widehat{L} is differentiable, Fermat’s rule gives

0∈∇L^​(M⋆λ)+λ​∂‖M⋆λ‖∗.0\in\nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\lambda\,\partial\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}.

Hence Eq. (11) holds for some S⋆∈∂‖M⋆λ‖∗S_{\star}\in\partial\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*}. Writing the compact SVD M⋆λ=P⋆​Σ⋆​Q⋆⊤M_{\star}^{\lambda}=P_{\star}\Sigma_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}, the standard subgradient formula for the nuclear norm yields

S⋆=P⋆​Q⋆⊤+W⋆,P⋆⊤​W⋆=0,W⋆​Q⋆=0,‖W⋆‖op≤1.S_{\star}=P_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}+W_{\star},\qquad P_{\star}^{\top}W_{\star}=0,\qquad W_{\star}Q_{\star}=0,\qquad\|W_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1.

Because ‖S~⋆‖op=‖S⋆‖op≤1\|\widetilde{S}_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|S_{\star}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1, we have I−S~⋆⪰0I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}\succeq 0. Moreover,

S⋆​V⋆=(P⋆​Q⋆⊤+W⋆)​Q⋆​Σ⋆1/2=P⋆​Σ⋆1/2=U⋆,S_{\star}V_{\star}=(P_{\star}Q_{\star}^{\top}+W_{\star})Q_{\star}\Sigma_{\star}^{1/2}=P_{\star}\Sigma_{\star}^{1/2}=U_{\star},

because W⋆​Q⋆=0W_{\star}Q_{\star}=0. Similarly,

S⋆⊤​U⋆=V⋆.S_{\star}^{\top}U_{\star}=V_{\star}.

Therefore

S~⋆​Z=[S⋆​V⋆S⋆⊤​U⋆]=[U⋆V⋆]=Z,\widetilde{S}_{\star}Z=\begin{bmatrix}S_{\star}V_{\star}\\ S_{\star}^{\top}U_{\star}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}U_{\star}\\ V_{\star}\end{bmatrix}=Z,

which proves Eq. (12). ∎

Lifted operators and differential identities.

We next rewrite the first- and second-order conditions of the factorized objective in lifted coordinates. The averaged operator below comes from expanding the matrix-space loss along the segment from M⋆λM_{\star}^{\lambda} to M=U​V⊤M=UV^{\top}; the pointwise operator is the Hessian that appears in the SOSP condition at the current factor pair. Both inherit the same lower and upper curvature constants after lifting, up to the balancing curvature.

Define the segment-average Hessian

H¯Δ​[H]:=∫01∇2L^​(M⋆λ+t​Δ)​[H]​𝑑t,\overline{H}_{\Delta}[H]:=\int_{0}^{1}\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t\Delta)[H]\,dt,

H¯~Δ​[E]:=[0H¯Δ​[E12]H¯Δ​[E12]⊤0],\widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E]:=\begin{bmatrix}0&\overline{H}_{\Delta}[E_{12}]\\ \overline{H}_{\Delta}[E_{12}]^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix},

and the composite lifted operator

ℋμ,Δavg​[E]:=2​H¯~Δ​[E]+2​μ​J​E​J.\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]:=2\widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E]+2\mu JEJ.

gμ,λ​(X):=4​hμ,λ​(U,V),GM:=∇L^​(M),G~M:=[0GMGM⊤0].g_{\mu,\lambda}(X):=4\,h_{\mu,\lambda}(U,V),\qquad G_{M}:=\nabla\widehat{L}(M),\qquad\widetilde{G}_{M}:=\begin{bmatrix}0&G_{M}\\ G_{M}^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}.

H~M​[E]:=[0∇2L^​(M)​[E12]∇2L^​(M)​[E12]⊤0],ℋμ,Xpt​[E]:=2​H~M​[E]+2​μ​J​E​J.\widetilde{H}_{M}[E]:=\begin{bmatrix}0&\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M)[E_{12}]\\ \nabla^{2}\widehat{L}(M)[E_{12}]^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[E]:=2\widetilde{H}_{M}[E]+2\mu JEJ.

A direct differentiation gives

12​⟨∇2gμ,λ​(X)​[D],D⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\bigl\langle\nabla^{2}g_{\mu,\lambda}(X)[D],D\bigr\rangle =⟨2​G~M+2​μ​J​X​X⊤​J+2​λ​I,D​D⊤⟩\displaystyle=\Bigl\langle 2\widetilde{G}_{M}+2\mu JXX^{\top}J+2\lambda I,\;DD^{\top}\Bigr\rangle (14)
+12​⟨ℋμ,Xpt​[D​X⊤+X​D⊤],D​X⊤+X​D⊤⟩.\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\Bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[DX^{\top}+XD^{\top}],\;DX^{\top}+XD^{\top}\Bigr\rangle. (15)

By the pathwise rank-kk RSC/RSS assumption for the candidate product MM, the curvature bounds apply along the segment {M⋆λ+t​Δ:t∈[0,1]}\{M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t\Delta:t\in[0,1]\} and at the current point MM corresponding to t=1t=1. In particular, let

mμ\displaystyle m_{\mu} :=2​min⁡{μ,αk−μ},Lμ:=2​max⁡{μ,βk−μ},\displaystyle:=2\min\{\mu,\alpha_{k}-\mu\},\quad L_{\mu}:=2\max\{\mu,\beta_{k}-\mu\},
κμ\displaystyle\kappa_{\mu} :=Lμmμ,sμ:=Lμ+mμ2,dμ:=Lμ−mμ2.\displaystyle:=\frac{L_{\mu}}{m_{\mu}},\quad s_{\mu}:=\frac{L_{\mu}+m_{\mu}}{2},\quad d_{\mu}:=\frac{L_{\mu}-m_{\mu}}{2}.

For a lifted symmetric matrix

B=[B11B12B12⊤B22]B=\begin{bmatrix}B_{11}&B_{12}\\ B_{12}^{\top}&B_{22}\end{bmatrix}

with rank⁡(B12)≤k\operatorname{rank}(B_{12})\leq k, the RSC/RSS assumption and the identity ⟨J​B​J,B⟩=‖B11‖F2+‖B22‖F2−2​‖B12‖F2\langle JBJ,B\rangle=\|B_{11}\|_{F}^{2}+\|B_{22}\|_{F}^{2}-2\|B_{12}\|_{F}^{2} give

mμ​‖E‖F2≤⟨ℋμ,Δavg​[E],E⟩≤Lμ​‖E‖F2m_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2}\leq\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E],E\bigr\rangle\leq L_{\mu}\|E\|_{F}^{2} (16)

for every lifted symmetric matrix EE whose off-diagonal block has rank at most kk. The same calculation at the point MM gives

mμ​‖H‖F2≤⟨ℋμ,Xpt​[H],H⟩≤Lμ​‖H‖F2m_{\mu}\|H\|_{F}^{2}\leq\bigl\langle\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\mu,X}[H],H\bigr\rangle\leq L_{\mu}\|H\|_{F}^{2} (17)

for every lifted direction HH whose off-diagonal block has rank at most kk.

The next decomposition is the algebraic hinge of the proof. It rewrites the first-order expression at XX as the sum of a curvature term applied to the lifted error EE and a PSD slack Nμ,λN_{\mu,\lambda}. The slack is harmless in the later upper bounds because it is positive semidefinite and annihilates ZZ.

Lemma B.2 (Exact decomposition with KKT slack).

Define

Nμ,λ:=2​μ​J​Z​Z⊤​J+2​λ​(I−S~⋆).N_{\mu,\lambda}:=2\mu JZZ^{\top}J+2\lambda(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}).

Then

2​G~M+2​μ​J​X​X⊤​J+2​λ​I=ℋμ,Δavg​[E]+Nμ,λ.2\widetilde{G}_{M}+2\mu JXX^{\top}J+2\lambda I=\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{avg}}_{\mu,\Delta}[E]+N_{\mu,\lambda}. (18)

Moreover,

Nμ,λ⪰0,Nμ,λ​Z=0.N_{\mu,\lambda}\succeq 0,\qquad N_{\mu,\lambda}Z=0. (19)
Proof.

By the fundamental theorem of calculus,

GM=∇L^​(M⋆λ)+H¯Δ​[Δ].G_{M}=\nabla\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\overline{H}_{\Delta}[\Delta].

Using Eq. (11), this becomes

GM=−λ​S⋆+H¯Δ​[Δ].G_{M}=-\lambda S_{\star}+\overline{H}_{\Delta}[\Delta].

Since E12=ΔE_{12}=\Delta, we have

2​G~M=−2​λ​S~⋆+2​H¯~Δ​[E].2\widetilde{G}_{M}=-2\lambda\widetilde{S}_{\star}+2\widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E].

Also,

J​X​X⊤​J=J​E​J+J​Z​Z⊤​J.JXX^{\top}J=JEJ+JZZ^{\top}J.

Substituting these identities yields

2​G~M+2​μ​J​X​X⊤​J+2​λ​I=2​H¯~Δ​[E]+2​μ​J​E​J+2​μ​J​Z​Z⊤​J+2​λ​(I−S~⋆),2\widetilde{G}_{M}+2\mu JXX^{\top}J+2\lambda I=2\widetilde{\overline{H}}_{\Delta}[E]+2\mu JEJ+2\mu JZZ^{\top}J+2\lambda(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}),

which is Eq. (18).

By Eq. (12), I−S~⋆⪰0I-\widetilde{S}_{\star}\succeq 0 and (I−S~⋆)​Z=0(I-\widetilde{S}_{\star})Z=0. Also, (J​Z)​(J​Z)⊤⪰0(JZ)(JZ)^{\top}\succeq 0 and

(J​Z)​(J​Z)⊤​Z=J​Z​(Z⊤​J​Z)=0(JZ)(JZ)^{\top}Z=JZ(Z^{\top}JZ)=0

because Z⊤​J​Z=0Z^{\top}JZ=0. Therefore Eq. (19) follows. ∎

B.3.1 Admissible Loss Class and Universal Envelope

The direct theorem proof can be carried out using only the actual empirical loss L^\widehat{L}. For the Section 5 interface, however, it is helpful to separate the certificate calculation from the specific loss and retain only the matrix-space target condition and curvature bounds actually used by the argument.

For the fixed pair (X,Z)(X,Z), define the matrix-space path

Mt:=M⋆λ+t​Δ,t∈[0,1].M_{t}:=M_{\star}^{\lambda}+t\Delta,\qquad t\in[0,1].

Relative to the fixed curvature parameters (αk,βk)(\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}) and a rank level k≥r+r⋆k\geq r+r_{\star}, define the admissible loss class

ℱλ,αk,βk(k)​(X,Z):={h∈C2​(ℝn1×n2,ℝ):M⋆λ∈argminM[h⁡(M)+λ​‖M‖∗],αk​‖H‖F2≤⟨∇2h​(Mt)​[H],H⟩≤βk​‖H‖F2,for all ​t∈[0,1]​ and all ​H​ with ​rank⁡(H)≤k}.\mathcal{F}_{\lambda,\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}}^{(k)}(X,Z):=\left\{\begin{aligned} h\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}};\mathbb{R})\ :\ &M_{\star}^{\lambda}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M}\bigl[h(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*}\bigr],\\ &\alpha_{k}\|H\|_{F}^{2}\leq\langle\nabla^{2}h(M_{t})[H],H\rangle\leq\beta_{k}\|H\|_{F}^{2},\\ &\text{for all }t\in[0,1]\text{ and all }H\text{ with }\operatorname{rank}(H)\leq k\end{aligned}\right\}. (20)

For each h∈ℱλ,αk,βk(k)​(X,Z)h\in\mathcal{F}_{\lambda,\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}}^{(k)}(X,Z), let

gμ,λh​(X):=4​(h⁡(U​V⊤)+μ4​‖U⊤​U−V⊤​V‖F2+λ2​(‖U‖F2+‖V‖F2))g_{\mu,\lambda}^{h}(X):=4\left(h(UV^{\top})+\frac{\mu}{4}\|U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V\|_{F}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\right)

Proof of Proposition 4.3.

Let M:=U​V⊤M:=UV^{\top} and G:=∇L^​(M)G:=\nabla\widehat{L}(M). First-order stationarity of h~λ\widetilde{h}_{\lambda} gives

G​V+λ​U=0,G⊤​U+λ​V=0.GV+\lambda U=0,\qquad G^{\top}U+\lambda V=0.

U⊤​G​V−V⊤​G⊤​U+λ⁡(U⊤​U−V⊤​V)=0.U^{\top}GV-V^{\top}G^{\top}U+\lambda(U^{\top}U-V^{\top}V)=0.

If A:=U⊤​G​VA:=U^{\top}GV, then the first term is A−A⊤A-A^{\top}, which is skew-symmetric, whereas U⊤​U−V⊤​VU^{\top}U-V^{\top}V is symmetric. Their sum is zero, so both terms must vanish. Hence

U⊤​U=V⊤​V.U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V.

If (U,V)(U,V) is an SOSP of h~λ\widetilde{h}_{\lambda}, then adding μ​R\mu R preserves both first-order stationarity and second-order nonnegativity. Thus (U,V)(U,V) is also an SOSP of hμ,λh_{\mu,\lambda} for every μ≥0\mu\geq 0. ∎

Proof of Corollary 4.4.

Fix the same parameter μ∈(0,αk)\mu\in(0,\alpha_{k}) as in Theorem 4.2. By Proposition 4.3, every SOSP of the standard LoRA objective Eq. (1) is also an SOSP of the balanced objective Eq. (2). Theorem 4.2 therefore gives

U​V⊤=M⋆λ.UV^{\top}=M_{\star}^{\lambda}.

At this point, the balancing penalty vanishes, so

h~λ​(U,V)=L^​(M⋆λ)+λ2​(‖U‖F2+‖V‖F2)=L^​(M⋆λ)+λ​‖M⋆λ‖∗,\widetilde{h}_{\lambda}(U,V)=\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl(\|U\|_{F}^{2}+\|V\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)=\widehat{L}(M_{\star}^{\lambda})+\lambda\|M_{\star}^{\lambda}\|_{*},

where the last equality follows from the balanced square-root characterization of M⋆λM_{\star}^{\lambda}. Hence the standard LoRA factor pair attains the same value as the optimal rank-constrained matrix-space problem, so it is globally optimal for the standard LoRA objective as well. ∎

Appendix C Additional Proofs for Section 5

This appendix section follows the notation of Section 5. The empirical distribution ν\nu over supervised prediction instances defines L^ν\widehat{L}_{\nu}. We first specify the certificate region and admissible family underlying the data-side bounds, then derive the cross-entropy identities and curvature certificate. Recall that xx denotes a supervised prediction instance induced by the original examples, zx​(M)z_{x}(M) is the model’s pre-softmax logit vector for this instance, px​(M)=softmax⁡(zx​(M))p_{x}(M)=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{x}(M)) is the predicted probability vector, and qxq_{x} is the target probability vector. We also write

Qν​(M,H):=𝔼ν​‖P⟂​Ax,M​[H]‖22Q_{\nu}(M,H):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H]\|_{2}^{2}

for the projected, unweighted coverage form.

C.1 Certificate Region and Admissible Family

Fix the empirical distribution ν\nu, search rank rr, and a regularized target Mν,⋆λM_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda} from Assumption 3.1, with rν,⋆=rank⁡(Mν,⋆λ)≤rr_{\nu,\star}=\operatorname{rank}(M_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda})\leq r. Let

ℳr:={M∈ℝn1×n2:rank⁡(M)≤r}.\mathcal{M}_{r}:=\{M\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}:\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r\}.

The certificate region collects the target–candidate segments in Assumption 4.1:

ℳcert(ν,r):={(1−t)Mν,⋆λ+tM:M∈ℳr,t∈[0,1]}.\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cert}}(\nu,r):=\bigl\{(1-t)M_{\nu,\star}^{\lambda}+tM:M\in\mathcal{M}_{r},\ t\in[0,1]\bigr\}. (35)

For k≥r+rν,⋆k\geq r+r_{\nu,\star}, define the admissible family

𝒯k​(ν,r):={(M~,H):M~∈ℳcert​(ν,r),H∈ℝn1×n2,rank⁡(H)≤k,‖H‖F=1}.\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r):=\left\{\begin{aligned} (\widetilde{M},H):\ &\widetilde{M}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cert}}(\nu,r),\\ &H\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}},\quad\operatorname{rank}(H)\leq k,\quad\|H\|_{F}=1\end{aligned}\right\}. (36)

Thus the matrix points include both endpoints and the full intervening segments, while HH ranges over all unit rank-at-most-kk directions. The segment points can have rank up to r+rν,⋆r+r_{\nu,\star}, even though each candidate update has rank at most rr. For a candidate-specific application, the same definitions may be restricted to the single segment joining that candidate to the target; the resulting bounds then apply to that candidate. Unless stated otherwise, the quantities below use the full family 𝒯k​(ν,r)\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r) defined above.

The coverage bounds and nonlinear residual bound are

cν,k\displaystyle c_{\nu,k} :=inf(M,H)∈𝒯k​(ν,r)Qν​(M,H),Cν,k:=sup(M,H)∈𝒯k​(ν,r)Qν​(M,H),\displaystyle:=\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}Q_{\nu}(M,H),\qquad C_{\nu,k}:=\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}Q_{\nu}(M,H), (37)
ρν,k\displaystyle\rho_{\nu,k} :=sup(M,H)∈𝒯k​(ν,r)|Rν​(M,H)|.\displaystyle:=\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}|R_{\nu}(M,H)|. (38)

To define the softmax-weighting bounds, set

𝒯k+​(ν,r):={(M,H)∈𝒯k​(ν,r):Qν​(M,H)>0}.\mathcal{T}_{k}^{+}(\nu,r):=\{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r):Q_{\nu}(M,H)>0\}.

C.2 Cross-Entropy Hessian Decomposition

Proposition C.1 (Cross-entropy Hessian).

Let zx​(M)∈ℝKz_{x}(M)\in\mathbb{R}^{K} be the pre-softmax logits for supervised instance xx, let px​(M):=softmax⁡(zx​(M))p_{x}(M):=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{x}(M)) be the predicted probabilities, and let qx∈ΔK−1q_{x}\in\Delta^{K-1} be the target probabilities. Define

ℓx​(M):=−⟨qx,log⁡px​(M)⟩.\ell_{x}(M):=-\langle q_{x},\log p_{x}(M)\rangle.

For any matrix direction HH, define the first- and second-order logit responses

Ax,M​[H]:=D​zx​(M)​[H],ℬx,M​[H,H]:=D2​zx​(M)​[H,H],A_{x,M}[H]:=Dz_{x}(M)[H],\qquad\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H]:=D^{2}z_{x}(M)[H,H],

and define the softmax covariance matrix Ωx​(M):=Diag⁡(px​(M))−px​(M)​px​(M)⊤\Omega_{x}(M):=\operatorname{Diag}(p_{x}(M))-p_{x}(M)p_{x}(M)^{\top}. Then

D2​ℓx​(M)​[H,H]=⟨Ax,M​[H],Ωx​(M)​Ax,M​[H]⟩+⟨px​(M)−qx,ℬx,M​[H,H]⟩.D^{2}\ell_{x}(M)[H,H]=\langle A_{x,M}[H],\Omega_{x}(M)A_{x,M}[H]\rangle+\langle p_{x}(M)-q_{x},\mathcal{B}_{x,M}[H,H]\rangle.

⟨∇2L^ν​(M)​[H],H⟩=Gν​(M,H)+Rν​(M,H),\langle\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}_{\nu}(M)[H],H\rangle=G_{\nu}(M,H)+R_{\nu}(M,H),

with GνG_{\nu} and RνR_{\nu} as defined in Section 5.

Proof.

For ϕ⁡(z,q):=−⟨q,log⁡softmax⁡(z)⟩\phi(z,q):=-\langle q,\log\operatorname{softmax}(z)\rangle, one has

∇zϕ​(z,q)=p−q,∇z2ϕ​(z,q)=Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤.\nabla_{z}\phi(z,q)=p-q,\qquad\nabla_{z}^{2}\phi(z,q)=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top}.

Applying the second-order chain rule to ℓx​(M)=ϕ⁡(zx​(M),qx)\ell_{x}(M)=\phi(z_{x}(M),q_{x}) gives the displayed identity. Since Ωx​(M)​𝟏=0\Omega_{x}(M)\mathbf{1}=0, common shifts of all logits are ignored by the Gauss–Newton term. Averaging over x∼νx\sim\nu gives the identity for L^ν\widehat{L}_{\nu}. ∎

Together with |Rν​(M,H)|≤ρν,k|R_{\nu}(M,H)|\leq\rho_{\nu,k}, the Hessian decomposition in Proposition C.1 implies

ων,k−​cν,k−ρν,k≤⟨∇2L^ν​(M)​[H],H⟩≤ων,k+​Cν,k+ρν,k.\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}-\rho_{\nu,k}\leq\langle\nabla^{2}\widehat{L}_{\nu}(M)[H],H\rangle\leq\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\rho_{\nu,k}.

By homogeneity, the same bounds hold for non-unit directions after multiplying by ‖H‖F2\|H\|_{F}^{2}. Therefore the data induce valid restricted curvature constants

αν,kCE=ων,k−​cν,k−ρν,k,βν,kCE=ων,k+​Cν,k+ρν,k.\alpha_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{CE}}=\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}-\rho_{\nu,k},\qquad\beta_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{CE}}=\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\rho_{\nu,k}.

Substituting these constants into the symmetric LoRA-RIP normalization (β−α)/(β+α)(\beta-\alpha)/(\beta+\alpha) gives

δν,kLoRA≤δ¯ν,kLoRA=ων,k+​Cν,k−ων,k−​cν,k+2​ρν,kων,k+​Cν,k+ων,k−​cν,k,\delta_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}\leq\overline{\delta}_{\nu,k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}=\frac{\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}-\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}+2\rho_{\nu,k}}{\omega_{\nu,k}^{+}C_{\nu,k}+\omega_{\nu,k}^{-}c_{\nu,k}},

which is Eq. (9). Plugging this conservative value into Theorem 4.2 yields the rank budget stated in the main text.

C.4 Mode Imbalance and Duplicate Sampling

Proposition C.2 (Group mass controls coverage conditioning).

A group mixture means the following two-stage sampling distribution: first choose a group g∈{1,…,G}g\in\{1,\ldots,G\} with probability πg\pi_{g}, and then draw x∼νgx\sim\nu_{g}. Equivalently, νπ=∑g=1Gπg​νg\nu_{\pi}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}\nu_{g}. Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the admissible comparison family for the mixture, for example 𝒯k​(νπ,r)\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu_{\pi},r). For every fixed (M,H)∈𝒯(M,H)\in\mathcal{T},

Qνπ​(M,H)=∑g=1Gπg​Qνg​(M,H),Gνπ​(M,H)=∑g=1Gπg​Gνg​(M,H).Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}Q_{\nu_{g}}(M,H),\qquad G_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{g}G_{\nu_{g}}(M,H).

Let (M+,H+)∈𝒯(M_{+},H_{+})\in\mathcal{T} be a direction strongly excited by group g+g_{+}, and define

U+:=Qνg+​(M+,H+).U_{+}:=Q_{\nu_{g_{+}}}(M_{+},H_{+}).

Let (M−,H−)∈𝒯(M_{-},H_{-})\in\mathcal{T} be a direction that is weakly covered under the mixture. For a possibly different group g−g_{-}, define its weak-direction contribution and the leakage from the other groups by

L−:=Qνg−​(M−,H−),ε−​(π):=∑j≠g−πj​Qνj​(M−,H−).L_{-}:=Q_{\nu_{g_{-}}}(M_{-},H_{-}),\qquad\varepsilon_{-}(\pi):=\sum_{j\neq g_{-}}\pi_{j}Q_{\nu_{j}}(M_{-},H_{-}).

The leakage term ε−​(π)\varepsilon_{-}(\pi) is small when the groups are well separated in their projected logit-response directions. Then

sup(M,H)∈𝒯Qνπ​(M,H)≥πg+​U+,inf(M,H)∈𝒯Qνπ​(M,H)≤Qνπ​(M−,H−)=πg−​L−+ε−​(π).\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)\geq\pi_{g_{+}}U_{+},\qquad\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)\leq Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M_{-},H_{-})=\pi_{g_{-}}L_{-}+\varepsilon_{-}(\pi).

Consequently, if the denominator below is positive,

sup(M,H)∈𝒯Qνπ​(M,H)inf(M,H)∈𝒯Qνπ​(M,H)≥πg+​U+πg−​L−+ε−​(π).\frac{\sup_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)}{\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)}\geq\frac{\pi_{g_{+}}U_{+}}{\pi_{g_{-}}L_{-}+\varepsilon_{-}(\pi)}.

In words, a dataset can have poor coverage conditioning when too much mass is concentrated on a mode that already gives large coverage response, while another mode receives too little mass and is not covered by the remaining groups. Duplicate samples are the limiting case in which one mode is a single atom: they reinforce the projected logit-response directions excited by that atom rather than increasing coverage uniformly.

Proof.

Linearity of expectation gives

Qνπ​(M,H)=∑j=1Gπj​Qνj​(M,H),Gνπ​(M,H)=∑j=1Gπj​Gνj​(M,H).Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{j=1}^{G}\pi_{j}Q_{\nu_{j}}(M,H),\qquad G_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)=\sum_{j=1}^{G}\pi_{j}G_{\nu_{j}}(M,H).

Evaluating the QQ-identity at (M+,H+)(M_{+},H_{+}) and using nonnegativity gives the upper-side bound. Evaluating it at (M−,H−)(M_{-},H_{-}) gives inf(M,H)∈𝒯Qνπ​(M,H)≤Qνπ​(M−,H−)=πg−​L−+ε−​(π)\inf_{(M,H)\in\mathcal{T}}Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M,H)\leq Q_{\nu_{\pi}}(M_{-},H_{-})=\pi_{g_{-}}L_{-}+\varepsilon_{-}(\pi). The ratio bound follows by combining the two inequalities. ∎

C.5 Gradient-Sketch Proxy for Experiments

At a fixed operating point M0M_{0}, the Gauss–Newton term can be viewed as a covariance on vectorized LoRA-update directions after they pass through the logit Jacobian. If h=vec⁡(H)h=\operatorname{vec}(H) and Jx,M0J_{x,M_{0}} is the matrix of the linear map H↦Ωx​(M0)1/2​Ax,M0​[H]H\mapsto\Omega_{x}(M_{0})^{1/2}A_{x,M_{0}}[H], then

Gν​(M0,H)=h⊤​(𝔼x∼ν​Jx,M0⊤​Jx,M0)​h.G_{\nu}(M_{0},H)=h^{\top}\left(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}J_{x,M_{0}}^{\top}J_{x,M_{0}}\right)h.

Thus any low-dimensional sketch that preserves the main modes of the logit Jacobian gives an empirical proxy for the weighted coverage spectrum. The gradient groups used in Section 6 should be read in this sense: they cluster examples by a margin-Jacobian sketch at a shared reference point. These sketches are not estimates of the exact constants cν,kc_{\nu,k}, Cν,kC_{\nu,k}, or ων,k±\omega_{\nu,k}^{\pm}, but they are aligned with the directions that enter the data-side certificate.

Proposition C.3 (Softmax covariance as variance).

For p∈ΔK−1p\in\Delta^{K-1}, Ω⁡(p):=Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤\Omega(p):=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top}, and any u∈ℝKu\in\mathbb{R}^{K},

u⊤​Ω​(p)​u=∑c=1Kpc​uc2−(∑c=1Kpc​uc)2=min⁡∑c=1Ka∈ℝ⁡pc​(uc−a)2.u^{\top}\Omega(p)u=\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_{c}u_{c}^{2}-\left(\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_{c}u_{c}\right)^{2}=\min_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_{c}(u_{c}-a)^{2}.

Proposition C.4 (Easy examples have limited Gauss–Newton leverage).

For p∈ΔK−1p\in\Delta^{K-1}, let pmax=1−δp_{\max}=1-\delta with δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1]. Then

λmax​(Ω⁡(p))≤tr⁡(Ω⁡(p))=1−‖p‖22≤2​δ−δ2.\lambda_{\max}(\Omega(p))\leq\operatorname{tr}(\Omega(p))=1-\|p\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\delta-\delta^{2}.

we have

Gx​(M,H)≤(2​δx−δx2)​‖Ax,M​[H]‖22,δx:=1−maxc⁡px,c​(M).G_{x}(M,H)\leq(2\delta_{x}-\delta_{x}^{2})\|A_{x,M}[H]\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\delta_{x}:=1-\max_{c}p_{x,c}(M).

Proposition C.5 (Directional saturation decomposition).

For any admissible (M,H)(M,H) with Qν​(M,H)>0Q_{\nu}(M,H)>0, define

σν​(M,H):=Gν​(M,H)/Qν​(M,H).\sigma_{\nu}(M,H):=G_{\nu}(M,H)/Q_{\nu}(M,H).

Then Gν​(M,H)=σν​(M,H)​Qν​(M,H)G_{\nu}(M,H)=\sigma_{\nu}(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H), and hence

inf𝒯k​(ν,r)Gν​(M,H)\displaystyle\inf_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}G_{\nu}(M,H) =inf𝒯k​(ν,r)σν​(M,H)​Qν​(M,H),\displaystyle=\inf_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}\sigma_{\nu}(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H),
sup𝒯k​(ν,r)Gν​(M,H)\displaystyle\sup_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}G_{\nu}(M,H) =sup𝒯k​(ν,r)σν​(M,H)​Qν​(M,H).\displaystyle=\sup_{\mathcal{T}_{k}(\nu,r)}\sigma_{\nu}(M,H)Q_{\nu}(M,H).

In a binary-margin parameterization, let mx​(M):=zx,1​(M)−zx,2​(M)m_{x}(M):=z_{x,1}(M)-z_{x,2}(M), let ϕx,M\phi_{x,M} be the Frobenius-Riesz representative of the linear map H↦D​mx​(M)​[H]H\mapsto Dm_{x}(M)[H], and set sx​(M):=px,1​(M)​px,2​(M)s_{x}(M):=p_{x,1}(M)p_{x,2}(M). Gν​(M,H)=𝔼ν​[sx​(M)​⟨ϕx,M,H⟩2],Qν​(M,H)=12​𝔼ν​⟨ϕx,M,H⟩2,G_{\nu}(M,H)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\bigl[s_{x}(M)\langle\phi_{x,M},H\rangle^{2}\bigr],\qquad Q_{\nu}(M,H)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\langle\phi_{x,M},H\rangle^{2},

for a softmax saturation weight sx​(M)≥0s_{x}(M)\geq 0.
