Directional saturation improves this curvature ratio only when the weighted mass increases the weak-direction floor more than it increases the ceiling.

Proof.

The first two identities are definitions. The binary-margin identities follow from Proposition C.3. For K=2K=2,

P⟂​Ax,M​[H]=12​D​mx​(M)​[H]​[1−1],‖P⟂​Ax,M​[H]‖22=12​(D​mx​(M)​[H])2,P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H]=\frac{1}{2}Dm_{x}(M)[H]\begin{bmatrix}1\\ -1\end{bmatrix},\qquad\|P_{\perp}A_{x,M}[H]\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(Dm_{x}(M)[H]\bigr)^{2},

which explains the factor 1/21/2 in QνQ_{\nu} under the centered-logit normalization used throughout the paper. The Gauss–Newton form retains the weight sx=px,1​px,2s_{x}=p_{x,1}p_{x,2}. The final statement follows by comparing the pure Gauss–Newton ratio: a nearly constant σν\sigma_{\nu} cancels in this ratio, whereas direction-dependent σν\sigma_{\nu} changes the ratio according to where it places weighted curvature mass. ∎

Appendix D Additional Experimental Details

This appendix records the protocols and full result tables for the rank sweeps and MNLI data interventions in Section 6. These tables report controlled single-seed runs. Appendix E presents multi-seed evaluations, landscape diagnostics, and robustness checks, with the settings specified for each study.

D.1 Shared Protocol

The MNLI/MPNet and CIFAR-100/ViT rank sweeps and MNLI data interventions use a controlled probe-then-LoRA protocol. We first train a linear classification head on the frozen backbone, and then keep this head fixed while fine-tuning only the pre-specified LoRA module. This is related to linear-probing-then-fine-tuning protocols, but differs from variants that continue updating the classification head during the fine-tuning stage  [Tomihari and Sato, 2024]. We keep the head fixed to isolate the effect of the LoRA update itself and keep the experiment close to the single-trainable-block setting analyzed in the main text. For the experiments in this appendix, unless stated otherwise, we use weight decay λA=λB=10−4\lambda_{A}=\lambda_{B}=10^{-4}, balancing coefficient μ=10−4\mu=10^{-4}, learning rate 10−410^{-4}, and the initialization scheme in which the AA-factor is Kaiming initialized with scale 0.010.01 and the BB-factor is initialized to zero. The train/validation split uses seed 1717, and the tables in this appendix use optimization seed 00. We use Adam with explicit weight decay for these runs. The diagnostic and robustness studies specify their seeds and protocol differences in Appendix E.

For the MNLI/MPNet experiments in this appendix, the train/validation/test sizes are 353,432/39,270/9,815353{,}432/39{,}270/9{,}815, the batch size is 3232, and the maximum sequence length is 128128. For CIFAR-100, the train/validation/test sizes are 45,000/5,000/10,00045{,}000/5{,}000/10{,}000, and the batch size is 6464. The MNLI rank sweep trains LoRA for 10 epochs; the CIFAR-100 rank sweep trains LoRA for 30 epochs; and the MNLI data-intervention runs train LoRA for 50 epochs on no-replacement subsets of 17,52617{,}526 examples.

D.2 Compute Resources

The experiment groups in Table D.2 were run with single-GPU training workers on NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada Generation GPUs with 4848 GB memory. Each rank or data condition was launched as an independent Python process on one GPU, without multi-node or distributed training. Up to four GPUs were used in parallel. For these runs, the observed GPU memory usage per LoRA or linear-probe worker was below 44 GB in nvidia-smi, and data loading used up to four CPU workers per process.

The hardware and memory measurements above apply to the experiment groups in Table D.2. Diagnostic and robustness protocols are described in Appendix E.

D.3 Rank Sweep Results

D.4 Gradient-Coverage Construction

The MNLI coverage experiment changes the data distribution without changing the subset size or label budget. The candidate pool is sampled once from MNLI train, and the final coverage proxy is defined by a gradient sketch with respect to the adapted matrix:

  1. 1.

    Use the frozen MPNet backbone and the trained linear-probe head as a shared reference point.

  2. 2.

    For each candidate example, choose the gold label and the strongest alternative label, and backpropagate the corresponding margin logit to the target query matrix.

  3. 3.

    Randomly project the activation and gradient-output factors to 16×1616\times 16, producing a 256256-dimensional bilinear sketch of the margin-Jacobian feature.

  4. 4.

    Normalize the sketches and cluster them within each label into eight groups, giving 24 label-conditioned gradient groups.

  5. 5.

    Draw no-replacement subsets of 17,52617{,}526 examples with the same label budget (5847,5788,5891)(5847,5788,5891) but different mass over these gradient groups.

The conditions are a balanced distribution with uniform mass over the eight groups within each label, and two geometric long-tail conditions with decay factors 0.750.75 and 0.450.45. Figure D.1 shows the resulting group masses.

D.5 Saturation-Band Construction and Results

The saturation-band experiment uses the same MNLI candidate pool and the same 24 label-conditioned gradient groups as the coverage experiment, but keeps the quota for every label–gradient group fixed. It therefore changes which examples are selected inside each group, rather than changing the mass assigned to the groups themselves. For each example, let pgoldp_{\rm gold} be the model probability of the gold label and let paltp_{\rm alt} be the largest non-gold class probability. We compute the pairwise softmax-curvature score

ppair=pgoldpgold+palt,s=ppair​(1−ppair).p_{\rm pair}=\frac{p_{\rm gold}}{p_{\rm gold}+p_{\rm alt}},\qquad s=p_{\rm pair}(1-p_{\rm pair}).

This reduces the multiclass prediction to the gold label versus its strongest competitor. In this pairwise view, if mx​(M)m_{x}(M) is the corresponding logit margin, the Gauss–Newton contribution has the form

Gν​(M,H)≈𝔼ν​[s​(D​mx​(M)​[H])2].G_{\nu}(M,H)\approx\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\!\left[s\,\bigl(Dm_{x}(M)[H]\bigr)^{2}\right].

Thus ss is the softmax-side curvature weight, while D​mx​(M)​[H]Dm_{x}(M)[H] determines the LoRA direction receiving that curvature. Within each fixed label–gradient group, we draw no-replacement examples from one of three quantile bands: easy, middle, and boundary. Table D.7 records the resulting score statistics, and Figure D.3 visualizes the separation between the three selected bands.

Appendix E Landscape Diagnostics and Robustness Evaluations

This section examines the optimization geometry and stability of LoRA fine-tuning through rank/checkpoint curvature, ambient matrix-space references, and multi-seed training. We also study the effects of data composition at a common reference point and along training trajectories, evaluate coverage across datasets, backbones, and adapter locations, and examine confidence-band selection on MNLI. The rank-sweep and MNLI data-intervention protocols are described in Appendix D.

Together, these evaluations connect rank-dependent optimization gains to data-induced geometry and the practical effectiveness of landscape-guided selection.

E.1 Shared diagnostic protocol

Unless stated otherwise, the diagnostics use MPNet-base on MNLI, a frozen linear-probe head, a frozen backbone, and a LoRA update on the layer-10 query projection. Every coverage condition contains 17,52617{,}526 unique training examples with label counts 5,847/5,788/5,8915{,}847/5{,}788/5{,}891. The shared data-aligned diagnostic basis has dimension 2424 and is obtained from the eight gradient-sketch groups within each of the three labels. Each ambient direction represented by this basis has rank at most 1616. The data-condition diagnostics use 512512 examples per label and three diagnostic-sample seeds.

The rank/checkpoint diagnostic uses ranks 4,64,128,2564,64,128,256, optimization seeds 0,1,20,1,2, and start, middle, and final checkpoints (epochs 0,5,100,5,10). It evaluates projected logit-Jacobian and CE-Hessian actions in the same 2424-dimensional basis. These actions are estimated by symmetric finite differences; a step-size check changes the projected matrices by at most 1.9%1.9\% and does not change the reported full-Hessian sign counts. Factor regularization and balancing Hessians are excluded when the ambient update MM is studied.

The data-condition diagnostic instead computes exact logit-JVP Gauss–Newton matrices and exact directional CE-HVPs in the common basis. The zero-update table uses the shared frozen probe point; the trajectory analysis evaluates matched rank-1616 checkpoints from the three training seeds. The reported means and standard deviations are over the three independent diagnostic or training seeds, as appropriate.

Theoretical constants and empirical diagnostics.

We do not directly compute exact values of δkLoRA\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}, r⋆r_{\star}, cν,kc_{\nu,k}, Cν,kC_{\nu,k}, ων,k±\omega_{\nu,k}^{\pm}, or ρν,k\rho_{\nu,k}. These quantities parameterize structural guarantees, rather than serving as per-run statistics. In classical matrix sensing and low-rank optimization, RIP relates measurement geometry to recovery and landscape guarantees [Recht et al., 2010, Ge et al., 2017, Zhang et al., 2021, Zhang, 2025b]. Its primary value in our framework is likewise the relationship it establishes between data geometry and rank requirements, not an isolated numerical constant for a particular run.

Exact certification is already computationally difficult for a fixed linear compressed-sensing matrix: the condition controls singular values across all supports of a prescribed size, and computing optimal RIP constants is NP-hard in general [Tillmann and Pfetsch, 2014]. Hardness also extends to approximate RIP certification [Weed, 2018]. For LoRA, the defining curvature bounds require uniform control over the continuous family of target-to-update segments and all admissible low-rank directions. Evaluating selected checkpoints in a diagnostic subspace does not compute these extrema. Likewise, determining r⋆r_{\star} requires identifying a global minimizer of the nonlinear regularized matrix-space objective FλF_{\lambda} and certifying its rank. Local optimization does not establish global optimality or uniqueness; r⋆r_{\star} refers to the low-rank target specified in our assumption. The matrix-space references and threshold or energy ranks reported below describe numerical solutions, not certified global targets.

The informative consequence of the analysis is how these quantities interact: The sufficient condition permits larger LoRA-RIP values at larger ranks, while coverage, softmax weighting, and nonlinear residual curvature enter the data-side certificate in explicit ways. Our experiments examine these mechanisms through controlled rank and data interventions, attained objectives, projected GN and CE-Hessian spectra, and multi-seed performance comparisons. The projected spectra characterize local geometry, rather than the theorem’s uniform LoRA-RIP constant. Lower attained objectives at larger ranks and the changes in geometry and performance under coverage and confidence-band selection provide complementary, qualitative evidence for the rank–data relationship developed by the theory.

E.2 Rank and checkpoint curvature

Table E.2 reports the full checkpoint measurements. The initial state is shared across ranks because the LoRA initialization has B=0B=0 and therefore M=B​A=0M=BA=0.

Ranks 6464–256256 reach positive CE-Hessian curvature throughout the shared projected subspace by the middle checkpoint and retain it at the final checkpoint, while rank 44 retains weak negative curvature. Final CE also decreases from 0.8390.839 at rank 44 to 0.7710.771 at rank 256256. Together, these trends link the gains from larger search ranks to lower-loss solutions with more favorable second-order geometry, consistent with the role of over-parameterization in our landscape analysis. Figure E.1 visualizes these trends.

E.3 Ambient matrix-space reference and effective rank

We obtain numerical matrix-space references by directly optimizing Fλ​(M)=Ltrain​(M)+λ​‖M‖∗F_{\lambda}(M)=L_{\mathrm{train}}(M)+\lambda\|M\|_{*} with λ=10−4\lambda=10^{-4}. We use full-batch gradients, FP64 singular-value thresholding, monotone backtracking, and two existing LoRA solutions as warm starts for each task. The threshold rank counts singular values above 10−4​σ110^{-4}\sigma_{1}; energy ranks count the number of directions needed to capture the indicated fraction of squared singular-value energy.

Table E.3 shows concentrated update energy: 99%99\% lies in 55–88 directions on MNLI and 2525–6262 on CIFAR-100. Table E.4 shows that increasing the search rank from 44 to 256256 reduces the best observed objective gap to the matrix-space reference from 0.064500.06450 to 0.002610.00261 on MNLI and from 0.046660.04666 to 0.000380.00038 on CIFAR-100. Together, the spectral summaries and shrinking objective gaps connect compact update structure with the optimization benefits of a larger search rank.

E.4 Multi-seed and subset-construction robustness

We repeat representative MNLI and CIFAR-100 rank experiments with three independent runs per rank. The runs jointly vary initialization, minibatch order, and stochastic training operations to measure the stability of the rank-dependent optimization and performance trends.

Across both tasks, larger ranks consistently achieve lower final factor objectives and higher mean validation accuracy. Within each rank, validation-accuracy standard deviations remain between 0.050.05 and 0.140.14 percentage points. The rank trends are therefore reproducible across training randomness, reinforcing the empirical connection between search rank and attainable objective quality. Figure E.2 shows the corresponding multi-run diagnostics.

Coverage stability across training and subset-construction seeds.

The Balanced-versus-Heavy comparison on MNLI also evaluates sensitivity to training randomness and subset construction. Across six ranks from 44 to 256256 with three training seeds, Balanced has higher validation accuracy at all six ranks. With independently reconstructed subsets, Heavy falls below Balanced in all 1212 paired runs. This consistency across both sources of randomness shows that preserving gradient-group coverage yields reliable improvements under a fixed data budget.

E.5 Projected data-condition diagnostics

The coverage diagnostic compares the balanced, light long-tail, and heavy long-tail subsets under the same label budget and subset size. The projected GN condition number is the ratio of the largest to smallest eigenvalue in the shared span. Stable rank is computed from the projected GN spectrum, and the residual norm is the operator norm of the nonlinear CE-Hessian residual in that span.

Balanced yields the lowest projected GN condition number and the highest stable rank. With GN floors on comparable scales, the lower ceiling identifies reduced concentration in dominant directions as the main source of better conditioning. Balanced also has a smaller nonlinear residual. These results support the coverage mechanism: spreading the data budget across response modes produces more even directional support and a more favorable curvature profile.

Figure E.3 displays the corresponding GN condition numbers and curvature spectra.

E.6 CE-Hessian geometry along training

We compare the projected CE-Hessian geometry reached by Balanced, Light, and Heavy training at start, middle, and final checkpoints, using the same 1,5361{,}536-example diagnostic set and 2424-dimensional basis. Figure E.4 focuses on the minimum CE-Hessian eigenvalue and the number of negative eigenvalues in this shared subspace. Table E.7 records the complete checkpoint measurements.

Balanced reaches a positive mean minimum CE-Hessian eigenvalue by the middle checkpoint, and all three training runs have zero detected negative eigenvalues at both the middle and final checkpoints. At the final checkpoint, Light and Heavy retain an average of 3.003.00 and 4.334.33 negative eigenvalues, respectively. This consistent separation links balanced gradient-group coverage to training states with more favorable local second-order geometry, complementing the common-reference coverage analysis.

E.7 Confidence-band diagnostics and multi-seed evaluation

The MNLI confidence-band comparison fixes subset size, label counts, and gradient-group quotas. The score is s=ppair​(1−ppair)s=p_{\rm pair}(1-p_{\rm pair}), where ppair=pgold/(pgold+palt)p_{\rm pair}=p_{\rm gold}/(p_{\rm gold}+p_{\rm alt}). All bands are evaluated at the same zero-update model in the common 24-dimensional span. This tests whether changing average pairwise confidence mainly changes curvature scale or also changes projected conditioning.

With gradient-group quotas fixed, Middle and Boundary provide higher GN trace than Easy in all three diagnostic samples, while mean projected condition numbers remain close (32.4032.40–33.1633.16). This highlights the role of softmax weighting in the amount of curvature supplied to covered directions, rather than a clear conditioning advantage for a particular band. The training comparisons below separately evaluate how these confidence-band choices affect fine-tuning performance.

Table E.9 shows that both Middle and Boundary improve mean validation accuracy over Easy at all four ranks, with smaller run-to-run variability. Their relative ordering varies: Middle leads at ranks 44 and 1616, the reported means tie at rank 3232, and Boundary has the highest mean at rank 6464. Together with the reference-point diagnostics, these results support confidence-aware selection that avoids concentrating the budget on highly saturated examples while maintaining directional coverage, rather than a universal preference for the middle band.

E.8 Cross-Backbone and Cross-Dataset Gradient Coverage

We extend the gradient-coverage intervention to a second backbone on MNLI and to QNLI with MPNet-base. Both experiments compare Balanced, Light long-tail, and Heavy long-tail sampling. Balanced assigns approximately equal example counts to the eight gradient groups within each label. At each rank, the three conditions share the same subset size, label budget, target module, and training settings; the intervention changes how the data budget is allocated across gradient groups. Both experiments use ranks r∈{16,64}r\in\{16,64\}, seeds 0,1,20,1,2, 50 training epochs, and batch size 32. Validation and test accuracies are evaluated at the checkpoint with the lowest validation cross-entropy in each run. The tables report three-seed summaries in percentage units.

DeBERTa-v3-base on MNLI.

We use microsoft/deberta-v3-base, with LoRA applied only to the layer-10 query projection and the existing linear-probe head kept fixed. Each selected subset contains 17,52617{,}526 examples, with label counts (5,847,5,788,5,891)(5{,}847,5{,}788,5{,}891). Normalized gradient sketches are clustered into eight groups per label, giving 24 label-conditioned groups. The Light and Heavy long-tail conditions use group-mass decay factors 0.600.60 and 0.450.45, respectively. The maximum sequence length is 128.

Table E.10 shows that Balanced achieves the highest validation and test accuracy at both ranks, followed by Light and then Heavy long-tail. Relative to Heavy long-tail, Balanced improves test accuracy by 2.182.18 percentage points at r=16r=16 and 1.621.62 points at r=64r=64. The Balanced-versus-Heavy advantage across MPNet and DeBERTa supports gradient-response coverage as a model-aware criterion for selecting fine-tuning data.

MPNet-base on QNLI.

We use microsoft/mpnet-base on QNLI, targeting the layer-10 attention query projection. Each condition contains 5,1255{,}125 examples with label counts (2,534,2,591)(2{,}534,2{,}591). Normalized gradient/margin-Jacobian sketches form eight groups per label, giving 16 label-conditioned groups. The model, adapted layer, total subset size, label budget, and training settings are held fixed across the three sampling conditions at each rank.

As shown in Table E.11, Balanced again outperforms Light long-tail, which outperforms Heavy long-tail, on both validation and test accuracy. Balanced improves test accuracy over Heavy long-tail by 5.505.50 percentage points at r=16r=16 and 6.796.79 points at r=64r=64. The sustained gains at both ranks show that allocating a fixed sample budget across complementary response groups remains valuable as the adapter capacity increases.

Across both evaluations, Balanced at rank 1616 outperforms Heavy at rank 6464, using only one quarter of the adapter rank. These comparisons show how better coverage can improve the effectiveness of a smaller adapter, directly supporting the joint consideration of data composition and rank in resource-efficient LoRA fine-tuning.

E.9 Adapter-location robustness

We evaluate the Balanced-versus-Heavy coverage comparison at several adapter locations on MNLI. For layers 5, 7, and 8, gradient sketches are recomputed at the corresponding query projection. The all-layer query/value run evaluates placement transfer using the fixed layer-10-selected subsets.

Balanced improves test accuracy at every tested location, by 0.8900.890–1.9391.939 percentage points for single-layer query adapters and 1.1241.124 points for all-layer query/value adaptation. The all-layer gain uses the fixed layer-10-selected subsets, showing that the coverage benefit transfers across adaptation configurations.

Appendix F Limitations

Our theoretical analysis focuses on single-matrix LoRA fine-tuning with cross-entropy loss under low-rank target and LoRA-RIP assumptions. The resulting rank bounds are sufficient rather than necessary, leaving room for tighter characterizations of the relationship between adapter rank and data-induced geometry. Our empirical evaluation examines this relationship through controlled classification experiments across datasets and backbones. Extending the theory to joint multi-layer adaptation and evaluating the data-selection principles in larger-scale generative fine-tuning are natural directions for future work.
